subject: Edge proxy ingress path: PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S VPN — decision brief
messages:

Subject: Edge proxy ingress path: PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S VPN — design kickoff

Team,

Quick kickoff for ArgusHealth: they want a clear recommendation and an operational checklist for connecting their on-prem / VPC-connected edge proxies to Redwood Private (single-tenant control plane in our VPC). The ask is: which ingress model should we propose for production and why — and what we recommend for PoC.

High level context:
- Customer (ArgusHealth) will place an edge proxy in their VPC that will forward inference requests to Redwood Private in our customer-dedicated account.
- Their infra team is open to PrivateLink, peering, or an S2S VPN + NAT gateway; they care about security, supportability, latency stability, and egress costs.

Please review the attached connectivity-matrix.xlsx for perf/cost/security tradeoffs and the quick questions below. I want to land on a recommended path and an ops checklist to give Argus by EOD Tue.

Questions to resolve before recommendation:
1) Does PrivateLink support our current streaming architecture without extra proxies (considering long-lived TCP connections and TLS passthrough)?
2) If peering is chosen, how do we handle IP address overlap and routing across multiple customer VPCs (transit gateway vs individual peering)?
3) For S2S VPN: is jitter and MTU degradation acceptable for our latency SLOs? Also -- egress billing implications?

Attachments: connectivity-matrix.xlsx (tabbed: latency, cost, security notes)

Next steps: Marcus, can you sanity-check the perf numbers vs our kernel-optimized runtimes? Kimberly, any infra/permission notes for supporting PrivateLink endpoints across accounts? I’ll loop in Argus NetOps for any missing network constraints.

Thanks,

Irene

Irene — quick read-through and a few notes inline. Attachment: topology-diagram.vsdx (simple sketch).

On Sun, Aug 29, 2026 at 09:03 AM Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.com> wrote:
> Team,
>
> Quick kickoff for ArgusHealth: they want a clear recommendation and an operational checklist for connecting their on-prem / VPC-connected edge proxies to Redwood Private (single-tenant control plane in our VPC).

My comments:
- PrivateLink: operationally this is the cleanest for cross-account access. We create an NLB in our customer-dedicated account, expose a Network Load Balancer-backed Interface Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) in Argus' VPC. Pros: no route table changes, no CIDR coordination, good security boundary. Cons: NLB has client IP preservation caveats when proxy protocol isn't used; also streaming long-lived connections are supported but we need to ensure our NLB idle timeouts are tuned (set to higher value) and health checks aligned with our runtime.

- Peering: best throughput and minimal extra hops — but requires non-overlapping CIDRs and peering scales poorly if we need many customer VPCs. If Argus intends multiple VPCs or cross-account workloads, recommend Transit Gateway rather than many pairwise peerings. Also note: peering does not support transitive routing, so if there’s a third-party security VPC in the path, complexity rises.

- S2S VPN: good quick PoC option. It is the least operationally predictable: jitter, MTU issues (path MTU discovery often fails with encapsulation), and encryption CPU on their gateways can introduce latency variance. Also, bandwidth caps on VPN appliances may be limiting for high-QPS inference. Billing-wise, S2S means traffic egress still incurs normal cloud egress; PrivateLink can sometimes reduce inter-AZ charges depending on region and path.

Minor infra notes:
- For PrivateLink, we must run the endpoint service in a multi-AZ NLB configuration to match SLOs.
- TLS termination: prefer our service to terminate TLS, but support TLS passthrough if Argus requires end-to-end client certs. If passthrough is used, the NLB must be TCP and we should not mutate TLS.
- IP whitelisting for control plane: we should provide a predictable set of ENIs or endpoint IDs for their firewall rules; include a small range and document update cadence.

I attached a simple topology and labeled where we'd place NLB vs peering vs VPN. Happy to sync with Marcus about kernel/connection behavior.

—Kimberly

Subject: Re: Edge proxy ingress path: PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S VPN — design kickoff

Thanks for the primer. A few clarifying items from our side before you land a recommendation:

1) IP overlap — Argus has a handful of legacy VPCs with overlapping /16 ranges (internal). We don’t want to re-CIDR. Does PrivateLink avoid that entirely?
2) BGP — If we move forward with Transit Gateway + peering, we want to run BGP between our physical edge and TGW for dynamic routes. Any constraints on path MTU or fragmentation if you expect large batched payloads?
3) Authentication / mTLS — Would Redwood be able to support mutual TLS on the application socket if we do PrivateLink with TCP passthrough?
4) Failover — For multi-region resilience we may have active/passive Redwood endpoints. How do you recommend failover be implemented w/ minimal DNS TTL flapping?

We can provision a VPN as a stopgap, but we will need a production design that avoids having to renumber.

—Sean (Argus NetOps)
From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.com>
To: Sean <netops@argushealth.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 29 Aug 2026 16:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Edge proxy ingress path: PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S VPN — design kickoff

Sean — good questions. Summary recommendation and operational notes below. I’ve also uploaded a short one-page checklist to the shared drive (link above).

TL;DR recommendation:
- Production: PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint backed by a multi-AZ NLB in our customer-dedicated account) as the primary ingress. Rationale: avoids CIDR renumbering, reduces attack surface (no route table changes), and supports cross-account access cleanly. We'll run TCP (NLB) with optional TLS passthrough to support mTLS.
- Multi-VPC / High-throughput use case: If Argus needs extremely high sustained throughput across many VPCs, use Transit Gateway with VPC attachments and a shared peering/TGW fabric. This requires non-overlapping CIDRs or a NAT/translation layer; if renumbering is impossible, TGW with multicast/translation appliances is an option but operationally heavier.
- PoC/short-term: Site-to-site VPN is acceptable to start, but treat it as a temporary path. Expect higher jitter and MTU shrinkage; do not rely on VPN to meet production latency SLOs.

Answers and Ops details: 
1) IP overlap: PrivateLink is the least intrusive — it places interface endpoints in your VPC; you do not need to change route tables or CIDRs. Traffic to the service endpoint flows over ENIs, avoiding peering/routing conflicts.

2) BGP/MTU: If you opt for TGW + BGP, we recommend MTU 1500 across the path where possible and enabling PMTU discovery. For VPN (especially with IPsec + UDP encapsulation), expect an effective MTU reduction ~50–80 bytes. For large batched requests we recommend chunking on the client and enabling TCP MSS clamping on their gateway.

3) mTLS: Yes — we can support mTLS with TLS passthrough. For PrivateLink with passthrough the NLB is TCP and we terminate TLS within our containers; for strict end-to-end mTLS we can present a hardened passthrough path and validate mutual certs in the runtime. We'll need Argus to share CA chain and cert rotation cadence.

4) Failover: Use weighted DNS + health checks for region routing, or prefer a control-plane-aware routing policy: we can advertise endpoint readiness via a small API and coordinate DNS updates with a low TTL (30s) for failover windows. If you prefer not to use DNS flapping, consider cross-region PrivateLink + health-proxy in their VPC that forwards to the currently-active Redwood endpoint.

Operational checklist (high level):
- For PrivateLink production:
  - Provision multi-AZ NLB in our customer-dedicated account, expose service via Interface Endpoint in Argus VPC.
  - Configure NLB idle timeout = 3600s (support long-lived streams).
  - Provide Argus a small ENI IP set (documented) + endpoint service name for firewall allowlist.
  - Share certs/rotation plan if using mTLS passthrough.
  - Test streaming at scale (0–1000 concurrent connections) during pilot window.

- For Transit Gateway option:
  - Validate CIDR overlaps. If overlaps exist, plan translation layer or renumbering.
  - Propose BGP peering between their edge and TGW for dynamic failover.
  - Document egress metering (TGW data processing) and cost responsibilities.

- For VPN PoC:
  - Establish IPsec tunnel, enable MSS clamping, run jitter/latency tests, set clear PoC expiration (30 days).

Next steps:
- Kimberly/Marcus: can you confirm the NLB idle timeout and connection preservation behavior with our runtime (Marcus — perf numbers vs long-lived streams)?
- Sean: if you can share the list of overlapping VPC CIDRs and their preferred cert rotation cadence I’ll incorporate into the final recommendation doc.

I’ll aim to push a one-page decision brief + an ops checklist by Tue EOD.

Best,
